fixes.explanation: Ben-hadad, king of Aram, sends word to Ahab, king of Israel: “Your silver and gold are mine, and your best wives and children are mine!” (1 Kings 20:3) Silver, gold, family. That's the whole list. Ben-hadad doesn't ask nicely, either.

No stalling here. The text just says the king of Israel replied, and what he says is, “Just as you say, my lord the king: I am yours, along with all that I have.” Ahab doesn't ask for a single day to think. It's a yes, and it covers everything Ben-hadad asked for.

Ahab summons “…all the elders of the land…” He tells them Ben-hadad is looking for trouble, because Ahab didn't deny him a single thing in the first demand. Smart move, calling in the whole table before answering.

The elders and the people all say, “Do not listen to him or consent to his terms.” That's a clear answer from everybody at the table. Ahab had already said yes to the first demand, and now the elders and the people tell him to refuse these terms. I think it's a crowd that has had enough.

Ben-hadad swears, “May the gods deal with me, and ever so severely, if enough dust remains of Samaria for each of my men to have a handful.” That's his threat: not enough dust left of Samaria for each of his men to take a handful. That's a lot of threat packed into one sentence. Remember that he's the one doing the swearing.

The text says Ben-hadad got Ahab's message “…while he and the kings were drinking in their tents…” That's thirty-three kings, counting Ben-hadad, in tents with cups. I think it's worth noticing where they are when that message reaches them. Hold that picture, because it comes back later in the story.

Praying? Not in this tent, friend. Ben-hadad received Ahab's message “…while he and the kings were drinking in their tents…” The kings are in their tents, and that's the word the text gives: drinking.

Ben-hadad hears Ahab's message and tells his servants, “Take your positions.” So they station themselves against the city. No long speech, no second oath. Just orders, and his servants take their places.

That's a quiet ending, but it's not what the prophet says. He brings this word from the LORD: “Behold, I will deliver it into your hand this very day, and you will know that I am the LORD.” The LORD says He will deliver the army into Ahab's hand. And He says it happens today.

The 232 are in front, but they have company. Ahab assembles “…the rest of the Israelite troops, 7,000 in all.” The text says the army is behind the young officers as they march out of the city. It's a small crew up front, with a bigger one at their backs.

It is true, and it's right there in the text. Ahab's troops marched out at noon “…while Ben-hadad and the 32 kings allied with him were in their tents getting drunk.” Midday, and the kings are in their tents. Meanwhile Israel's troops are already marching out.

Each of the young officers strikes down his opponent, “So the Arameans fled, with the Israelites in pursuit.” The word is fled. The Arameans were the ones with the big army and the oath about dust. Now they're the ones running.

Regrouping isn't what the text says. After each of the young officers strikes down his opponent, “…the Arameans fled, with the Israelites in pursuit.” They run, and Israel chases. That's the word the text gives: fled.
